Threat.value: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, the trigger pattern is not clinically well matched: 'Military Topics' suggests combat/war-related trauma cues, and 'Loss Themes' suggests bereavement-related reminders, while no trigger references fumes, smells, contamination, breathing difficulty, workplaces, or chemical hazards. This makes the trigger set hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The threat items are internally coherent with a persecution/assault-style danger formulation ('someone is following me', needing to stay alert at night) rather than a toxic exposure formulation. They do not plausibly connect to the selected triggers, despite the strong Triggers → Threat edge that should link these nodes tightly.

issues.item: Triggers: Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
issues.explanation: The trigger item about discussions of people losing loved ones is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of toxic chemical exposure. It implies bereavement-related trauma content that is not otherwise represented in the profile, making this trigger clinically implausible for the same patient unless the exposure involved deaths, which is not supported elsewhere.

Within the Threat node, concentration difficulty is a broad nonspecific symptom, whereas sleep vigilance reflects an ongoing sense of current external danger. That combination can coexist, but in this profile the threat content is otherwise sparse and the selected triggers do not clearly support a coherent toxic-exposure-related danger schema, weakening internal coherence.

vignette:
Fatima Khalil is a 51-year-old married woman of Lebanese descent who has worked in hotel management for nearly two decades. She presents for psychological assessment approximately fourteen months after a toxic chemical exposure incident that occurred at the large downtown hotel she manages, and which she describes as the most terrifying experience of her life.

The incident took place on a busy Tuesday morning during a routine inspection of the hotel's maintenance level. A contractor had been working with industrial cleaning agents in a poorly ventilated utility corridor, and when Fatima arrived to sign off on the work order, she walked directly into a cloud of aerosolized chemical compound. Within seconds her eyes were burning, her throat had closed to what felt like a pinhole, and she lost her footing against the wall, unable to call for help. She remembered the contractor's panicked face above her, the sharp antiseptic-chemical smell filling her lungs, and then the fluorescent lights of an emergency room ceiling. She spent three days hospitalized for chemical burns to her airways, and for weeks afterward her voice carried a rasp she was convinced would never fully leave her.

In the months that followed her discharge, Fatima returned to work because she believed she had no choice - the hotel was her responsibility and she had a staff of forty depending on her. But the building that had been her professional home for eleven years had become something she could no longer navigate without cost. The maintenance corridors remained off-limits to her; she reassigned all utility inspections to her deputy manager without ever fully explaining why. What had once been a source of pride - her hands-on presence in every corner of the property - quietly contracted. Her deputy noticed. Her husband noticed. Fatima told them both she was simply delegating more effectively now that she was at a senior level, and she had repeated this to herself often enough that she almost believed it.

The hotel environment itself had become a source of sustained alertness she could not switch off. On the floor, surrounded by the ordinary noise of a working hotel - a luggage cart dropping unexpectedly, a door slamming at the end of a corridor - Fatima found her body responding before her mind had time to assess the situation. Her heart would slam against her ribs and her hands would go cold and she would stand very still, scanning. She had come to believe that her body was simply doing what the situation required, that a hotel was a genuinely unpredictable environment and that staying alert was professional competence rather than anything else. But the alertness did not stop when she left the building. At night she lay beside her husband unable to let herself fall fully asleep, certain in a way she could not articulate that something required her attention. She had told him she was going through a stressful period at work, which was true, and he had accepted this.

What she found hardest to explain, even to herself, was the smell. Any antiseptic or clinical odor - the hand sanitizer dispensers in the hotel lobby, the cleaning products used on the bathroom fixtures, and above all the particular sharp scent of a hospital corridor - produced an immediate and overwhelming physical response that she experienced as entirely disproportionate and deeply humiliating. She had accompanied her husband to a routine cardiology appointment eight months ago and had stood in the hospital entrance, unable to move past the reception desk, her body rigid and her vision narrowing. She had told him she would wait in the car. She had not returned to a medical building since.

It was her husband who finally insisted she speak to someone, after she woke one night rigid and sweating and could not explain to him what had frightened her. What brought Fatima to the intake appointment was less any single crisis than a slow accumulation: the shrinking of her professional authority, the distance that had grown between her and her husband in the small hours of the night, and a private fear she had not yet named aloud - that she was not recovering, and that she may never fully return to the person she was before she walked into that corridor.
